title: Laws of Large Numbers
markdown:
## What this covers

The material supplied for this chapter is not a lecture: no slide deck and no transcript were
provided, and the one "notes" file behind it is an **index page** — David Aldous's mirror of
Pitman's Graduate Probability Notes, arranged section by section to match the table of contents of
Rick Durrett's *Probability: Theory and Examples* (3rd edition). Each heading below names a topic
and links out to a separate PDF/TeX note; the definitions, theorem statements and proofs live in
those linked notes, which are outside what was supplied here.

So this chapter does the one honest thing available: it reproduces the **map** of Chapter 1 —
the order in which the topics are meant to be taken, and exactly which named note covers which
piece — without inventing the mathematics that map points at. Read it as a table of contents with
working links, not as an exposition. Where a subsection has no linked note in the source, that is
recorded as a gap rather than filled in.

## 1.1–1.4: the objects a law of large numbers needs

Before any law of large numbers can be stated, the chapter first fixes the objects it is a
statement about. Four sections do this, in this order:

- **1.1 Definitions** — one linked note, [Function Spaces](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205A/FunctionSpaces.pdf).
- **1.2 Random Variables** — [Real Random Variables](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205A/real-random-variables.pdf),
  [Random Variables](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205A/random-variables.pdf),
  [Marginal Distributions](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205A/MarginalDistribution.pdf),
  [Probability Measures](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205A/probability-measures.pdf),
  [Probability Distributions](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205A/probdistn.pdf),
  [Density](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205A/Densities.pdf).
- **1.3 Expected Value** — [Expected Value](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205A/expected-value.pdf) and
  [Change of Variables](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205A/change-of-variable.pdf), with two named
  subsections: *1.3.1 Inequalities for Expected Value*, covered by
  [Integration Inequalities](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205A/integration-inequalities.pdf), and
  *1.3.2 Integration to the limit*, covered by
  [Integration and Limit](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205A/Integration-and-Limit.pdf). A third
  subsection, *1.3.3 Computing expected values*, is named in the index with no note linked to it.
- **1.4 Independence** — [Independence of Two Variables](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205A/independence-2var.pdf),
  [Independence of n Variables](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205A/independence-nvar.pdf), and
  [Kolmogorov's Zero-One Law](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205A/Kolmogorov-zero-one-law.pdf). Two
  named subsections, *1.4.1 Conditions for independence* and *1.4.2 Independence, distribution, and
  expectation*, carry no linked note. A third, *1.4.3 Constructing independent random variables*, links to
  [Product Spaces](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205A/product-spaces.pdf) and
  [Construction of Independent Random Variables](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205A/Construction-Independence.pdf).

That is the whole preparatory arc: random variables and their distributions, then expectation and
its inequalities, then independence, ending on the zero-one law — the last thing established before
the chapter turns to the laws of large numbers themselves.

## 1.5 Weak Laws of Large Numbers

The index breaks this section into three named stages, in this order:

1. *1.5.1 L² weak laws* — no note linked.
2. *1.5.2 Triangular arrays* — no note linked.
3. *1.5.3 Truncation of Random Variables* — linked to
   [Weak Law of Large Numbers](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205A/WLLN.pdf).

The ordering itself is the content available here: an $L^2$ case is treated first, then the setting
is generalised to triangular arrays, and truncation is the technique that carries the argument from
there to the single linked note stating the Weak Law of Large Numbers. What the truncation argument
actually does, and what hypotheses it removes, is in that note rather than in the index.

## 1.6 Borel–Cantelli Lemmas

Two linked notes: [Almost Sure Convergence](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205A/asconvergence.pdf)
and [Borel-Cantelli Lemmas](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205A/borel-cantelli.pdf). The pairing
of these two titles is itself informative about the chapter's structure: almost-sure convergence is
introduced immediately before the lemmas that are the chapter's standard tool for proving it, and the
Strong Law follows directly on the next page of the syllabus.

## 1.7 Strong Law of Large Numbers

One linked note, [Strong Law of Large Numbers](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205A/strong-law-large-numbers.pdf).
No subsections are named — in the index this is the shortest section in the chapter, sitting between
the almost-sure machinery built in 1.6 and the convergence-of-series material in 1.8.

## 1.8 Convergence of Random Series

Two linked notes, in this order: [Kolmogorov's Maximal Inequality](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205A/kolmogrov-maximal-inequality.pdf)
and [Kolmogorov's Three-Series Theorem](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/205A/kolmogorov-3-series-theorem.pdf).
Both are named after Kolmogorov and both are listed after the Strong Law, consistent with the usual
role of this material as a tool for proving strong laws under weaker hypotheses than the elementary
argument needs — but that role is not stated in the index itself, only the ordering is.

## 1.9 Large Deviations for the Strong Law of Large Numbers

This section title is the last one in the chapter, and it is the one exception to the pattern above:
**no note is linked to it at all.** The index names the topic and stops there.

- **Referred to but not contained**: every linked PDF/TeX note above — *Function Spaces*, *Real Random
  Variables*, *Random Variables*, *Marginal Distributions*, *Probability Measures*, *Probability
  Distributions*, *Density*, *Expected Value*, *Change of Variables*, *Integration Inequalities*,

  Zero-One Law*, *Product Spaces*, *Construction of Independent Random Variables*, *Weak Law of Large
  Numbers*, *Almost Sure Convergence*, *Borel-Cantelli Lemmas*, *Strong Law of Large Numbers*,

  definitions, theorem statements, proofs and examples for this chapter live; none of them was supplied

  reproduced in this chapter. No exercises were supplied either.
